claims.claim: (a) benchmark: mean CoT tokens eff2/base = 1.48 at low, 1.33 at medium, 0.91 at high; history: 1.21, 1.20, 0.81

History: 1.16, 1.17, 0.82. The median-CoT ratio at benchmark high is 0.79. The direction (low and medium longer, high shorter) holds under every one of these statistics.

claims.claim: (b) benchmark accuracy eff2 - base: low +0.028 (paired 95% CI excludes 0), medium 0.000, high -0.010
claims.comment: Reproduces. The low-effort gain sits almost entirely in GPQA: GPQA +0.079 (n=445), HLE +0.017 (n=469), MMLU-Pro -0.030 (n=300). It is the only one of the six set-by-level comparisons whose CI excludes 0; history low is +0.005 [-0.023, +0.033]. At high, base truncates 19.6% of benchmark samples at 16k tokens and eff2 truncates 16.7%; truncated samples count as wrong. On questions where neither model truncated (n=937), the high-effort difference is -0.015.

claims.claim: (c) the high-minus-low accuracy gap shrinks by 0.038 on benchmark (CI excludes 0) and by 0.017 on history (CI includes 0)
claims.your_numbers: Per-question (high - low) accuracy, base minus eff2. Benchmark: base gap +0.0560, eff2 +0.0181, shrink +0.0379, bootstrap 95% [+0.0115, +0.0634], normal [+0.0121, +0.0636]. History: base +0.0350, eff2 +0.0183, shrink +0.0167, bootstrap [-0.0233, +0.0567].
claims.comment: Reproduces. The shrink is arithmetically the +0.028 low gain plus the -0.010 high loss from (b). Truncation at 16k caps the high-effort accuracies (base 19.6%, eff2 16.7% truncated on benchmark). On untruncated samples, high accuracy is 0.631 for base and 0.597 for eff2, so the size of the gap depends on the token cap.

claims.claim: (d) the per-question log-length gap between high and low shrinks by a factor of about 0.66 (benchmark) and 0.71 (history)
claims.your_numbers: Mean per-question gap ln(mean CoT high) - ln(mean CoT low). Benchmark: base 3.1175, eff2 2.6949; the ratio of gaps is 0.8645 and exp(difference) is 0.6554 [0.624, 0.689]. History: base 3.3506, eff2 3.0050; ratio 0.8969, exp(difference) 0.7078 [0.653, 0.767]. Using the mean of per-sample ln L instead gives 0.7123 for history. Geometric-mean high/low length ratio: benchmark 22.6x -> 14.8x, history 28.5x -> 20.2x. Per-question OLS slope of eff2 gap on base gap: 0.640 (benchmark), 0.705 (history).
claims.comment: Marked false because of the wording; the 0.66 and 0.71 are real numbers. They equal exp(eff2 gap - base gap), which is how much the geometric-mean high/low length ratio shrinks (22.6x to 14.8x). The log gap itself only shrinks by a factor of 0.86 on benchmark and 0.90 on history, which is 0.42 and 0.35 nats. Read literally, the claim says eff2 lost about a third of its log-length range between levels. It actually lost 10-14%. Corrected wording: 'the per-question high/low CoT length ratio shrinks by a factor of 0.66 (benchmark) and 0.71 (history).' The OLS slope (0.64 / 0.71) is a different statistic that happens to land close to these values.

claims.claim: (e) at low on benchmark, the CoT growth is larger on questions base gets wrong at medium (ratio 1.60) than on ones it gets right (1.36)
claims.your_numbers: Easy (base correct at medium, n=626): 1.3556. Hard (base wrong at medium, n=588): 1.5990. Hard minus easy = +0.243, stratified bootstrap 95% [+0.104, +0.395]. Hard has many HLE questions: per dataset, HLE easy 1.682 (n=63) vs hard 1.684 (n=406); GPQA 1.329 (n=314) vs 1.485 (n=131); MMLU-Pro 1.300 (n=249) vs 1.510 (n=51). Reweighting easy to hard's dataset mix: easy 1.555 vs hard 1.599, difference +0.044, bootstrap [-0.20, +0.27]. On history at low (base-majority split at medium) the direction reverses: easy 1.22 (n=106), hard 1.18 (n=44).
claims.comment: The numbers reproduce, but dataset mix explains most of the gap. HLE has the largest CoT growth at low (1.68x) whether base gets it right or wrong. HLE is 69% of the hard group and 10% of the easy group. After standardising by dataset, the hard-minus-easy difference is about 0.04 and its CI includes 0. A within-dataset hard > easy pattern appears in GPQA and MMLU-Pro but not HLE, and the history set reverses it. Do not read this as eff2 adapting its low-effort length to question difficulty.

data_problems:
I found no structural problems.

- **Row counts:** rows.jsonl has 16,326 rows: 3 models x (150 history x 4 samples + 1,214 benchmark x 1 sample) x 3 levels. Benchmark is GPQA 445, HLE 469, MMLU-Pro 300.
- **Duplicates and gaps:** no duplicate (model, set, dataset, qid, effort, sample_idx) keys. No (model, set, dataset, qid, effort) unit is missing in any model. sample_idx is always 0-3 for history and 0 for benchmark. No qid appears in both history and benchmark.
- **Correctness labels:** I re-parsed every response with cotswitch.extract.parse_answer_with_source on the response text alone. No row has correct=True without a parseable answer. No question has conflicting gold letters across its correct rows. No row is marked wrong while its parsed answer equals that gold letter.
- **Unparseable rows:** 631 rows have no parseable answer, 610 of them at high effort on benchmark. All truncated rows (finish=length: base 244, eff1 173, eff2 210) have an empty response and correct=False. No row has an empty CoT.
- **Prompts:** both models go through the same effort_eval.py path, render(tok, prompts.question_block(it), effort), which uses the chat template's reasoning_effort and asserts 'Reasoning: <level>'. grpo_effort.py trains with the same render and question_block, so the eval prompt matches the training format. Prompt token ids are not stored in the rows, so I could not check token-level identity between the base and LoRA tokenizers directly.
- **Base rows were reused, not resampled:** base rows sit at file positions 0-7435, interleaved with eff1 rows (5399-10883), so they were sampled in the eff1 run. The eff2 rows (10884-16325) came from a later run that skipped base through the done-set check. The 10.89M sampled tokens in results/effort_eval.log match eff2's own CoT+response total of 10.83M, so the log comes from that eff2-only run. effort_eval.py and effort_base.py did not change between commits 39c9d8ec and 6c1777eb.
- **Design caveats (not bugs):** benchmark has one sample per question. At high effort the 16k cap truncates 19.6% of base and 16.7% of eff2 benchmark samples, and truncation counts as wrong. This shapes the high-effort accuracies in (b) and (c).

simplest_wrong_explanation:
eff2 did not learn better effort control. It narrowed the length range across the three levels: low CoTs got longer (1.48x mean, 1.36x geometric) and high CoTs got shorter (0.91x). Accuracy then moved with length the way base's own length-accuracy curve would predict.

- **(b) and (c):** more tokens at low gives +0.028, almost all of it from GPQA (+0.079, while MMLU-Pro is -0.030). Fewer tokens at high gives -0.010. The 0.038 gap shrink in (c) is just the sum of those two effects, and a 16k cap that truncates about 17-20% of high-effort samples also shapes it.
- **(d):** the 'factor 0.66' describes the high/low length ratio. The log gap itself shrinks only 14% on benchmark and 10% on history.
- **(e):** the hard > easy growth mostly reflects HLE. HLE grows most at low (1.68x) whether base gets it right or wrong, and it is 69% of 'hard' but 10% of 'easy'. Standardised by dataset, the difference is about 0.04 with a CI that includes 0, and the history set reverses it.

None of these results needs a difficulty-sensitive effort policy to explain it.

claims.claim: (a) eff1 mean CoT is about 0.7x base at every level and on both sets (benchmark 0.71/0.68/0.82, history 0.74/0.68/0.67), with similar ratios on easy (base medium correct) and hard questions, i.e. uniform compression.
claims.your_numbers: Ratio of means eff1/base, paired by question: benchmark 0.711 / 0.680 / 0.824, history 0.737 / 0.684 / 0.674. Ratio of medians: benchmark 0.643 / 0.712 / 0.695, history 0.706 / 0.669 / 0.663. Easy/hard ratios on benchmark (easy = base medium correct, n=626/588): low 0.737/0.684, medium 0.721/0.652, high 0.806/0.834. History reproduces n=85/65 only when easy means all 4 base medium samples correct: low 0.754/0.719, medium 0.682/0.685, high 0.717/0.649. claims.comment: All quoted numbers reproduce. Two caveats on the reading. (1) The benchmark high ratio of 0.82 does not fit 'about 0.7x at every level'. It is pulled toward 1 by the 16k cap: base truncates 238 high samples and eff1 169, and a pair that both truncate has a ratio near 1. Without truncated pairs the ratio is 0.75. (2) Compression is roughly uniform but not exactly. At benchmark medium, hard questions compress more (easy minus hard gap +0.069, CI excludes 0). claims.claim: (c) base on benchmark: accuracy low 0.451, medium 0.516, high 0.507; median CoT 152 / 636 / 3880; 19.6% of high samples truncated at 16,000 tokens (finish == 'length'), eff1 13.9%, eff2 16.7%.
claims.your_numbers: Base benchmark accuracy 0.4514 / 0.5157 / 0.5074 (n=1214 each). Median CoT 152.5 / 636.5 / 3879.5; these are even-length medians, and Python's round-half-even gives 152/636/3880. Truncated at high: base 238/1214 = 19.60%, eff1 169/1214 = 13.92%, eff2 203/1214 = 16.72%. Base medium also has 1 truncated sample (0.08%).
claims.comment: Reproduces within rounding. Truncation is concentrated on HLE (base: 137/469 = 29.2%) and GPQA (90/445 = 20.2%), against 11/300 = 3.7% on MMLU-Pro.

claims.claim: (d) Is base high's failure to beat medium on benchmark explained by truncation? Compute high accuracy on non-truncated samples and what fraction of truncated samples base gets right at medium on the same question.
claims.your_numbers: Base high accuracy on its 976 non-truncated samples is 0.631 (616/976), against 0.582 (568/976) for base medium on the same questions. None of the 238 truncated high samples is correct; base medium gets 58/238 = 24.4% of those questions right. Decomposition: +48 correct on non-truncated questions and -58 on truncated ones, net -10 (0.507 vs 0.516). Scoring each truncated high sample with medium's result would give high 0.555 vs medium 0.516. Same pattern for the trained models: eff1 non-truncated high 0.590 vs medium 0.523 on the same questions, medium 21.9% on its truncated questions; eff2 0.597 vs 0.564, medium 27.6%. By dataset, base high on non-truncated vs all high: GPQA 0.856 vs 0.683, HLE 0.190 vs 0.134, MMLU-Pro 0.862 vs 0.830. The truncated CoTs are not repetition loops: zlib compression ratio of the last 4000 chars has median 0.417 for truncated samples vs 0.425 for non-truncated samples with CoT over 8000 tokens, and none is below 0.15.
claims.comment: Yes: truncation accounts for the entire gap. The truncated questions are hard ones that medium usually also gets wrong (24%), but every truncated high sample scores 0, and that costs more than high gains elsewhere. One caveat: the non-truncated subset is chosen by high's own sample length (1 sample per question), which favors high, so 0.631 vs 0.582 overstates the advantage somewhat. The 0.555 counterfactual is a more conservative estimate and still beats medium. The base high < medium result is an artifact of the 16k budget, not evidence that extra reasoning stops helping.

data_problems:
No structural problems. There are 16,326 rows, exactly 3 models x (150 history x 4 samples x 3 levels + 1,214 benchmark x 1 x 3). Every (model, set, dataset, qid, effort) key has exactly the expected sample_idx set (0-3 for history, 0 for benchmark). There are no duplicate sample keys. Every model and level uses the same question set, and history (mmlu_pro_full) is disjoint from benchmark (GPQA 445 / HLE 469 / MMLU-Pro 300).

Correctness: I re-parsed each response independently and compared it with gold letters from cotswitch.data. The `correct` flag agrees on all 16,326 rows. 0 rows have correct=True without a parseable answer, 0 truncated rows are marked correct, and all gold letters fall within their option counts.

Unparseable rows: base 246, eff1 174, eff2 211. Almost all are finish=length with an empty response. Only 4 stop rows lack a parseable answer:
- base history qid 4812 high: the model ended after the analysis channel with an empty final message; the CoT ends "Thus output 'ANSWER: D'".
- base history 5003 low: 'ANSWER: (none of the above)'.
- eff1 benchmark mmlu_pro 53 low: 'ANSWER: (none)'.
- eff2 hle 386 low: a free-form physics answer.

Minor items: 16 rows (8 eff1, 8 eff2) give a letter beyond the option count and are correctly scored wrong. 3 correct eff2 rows were parsed by the reference/fallback regex rather than an explicit ANSWER line. One eff1 truncated row has cot_tokens=16004, which comes from re-encoding drift.

Prompts: rows do not store prompts, so I could not check them directly. effort_eval.py renders every model the same way: render() with the chat template's reasoning_effort, plus prompts.question_block. Training (grpo_effort.py) uses the same render() and an equivalent question block. One possible difference: the gpt-oss template inserts 'Current date: ' + strftime_now. Base and eff1 were sampled in one invocation and eff2 in a later one; eff2 is the last 5,442 rows, base was skipped through the done-set, and effort_eval.log's 10.89M sampled tokens matches eff2 alone. The script was committed at 04:37 UTC on 10-23 and rows.jsonl was last written at 06:26 UTC on 10-23, so all runs very likely share the date line 2026-10-23. That is inferred from timestamps, not checked against stored prompts.

Design caveats:
- One base sample set serves as the comparison for both trained models.
- The done-key ignores sample counts, so a rerun with different --samples would mix silently. It has not happened here.
- Benchmark has 1 sample per question.
- The 16k cap censors 14-20% of benchmark high samples, which affects both the CoT ratios and the high-level accuracies.

(2) The benchmark high CoT ratio of 0.82, which seems to break the 0.7x pattern: the cap clips base's long tail more than eff1's (238 vs 169 truncated). Without truncated pairs the ratio is 0.75.

For (b), formatting failures are ruled out: eff1 has 0 unparseable rows at benchmark medium, and the drop shows up on GPQA, HLE and MMLU-Pro alike. 'Uniform compression' holds only roughly.
